question.problem:
Find the solution to the inequality $\frac{x+6}{4}>\frac{2x}{3}.$

The solution is $x$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
First, we clear the rational expressions by multiplying both sides of the inequality by the lowest common positive multiple of the denominators:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+6}{4} & >\frac{2x}{3} \\ 12\cdot (\frac{x+6}{4}) & >12\cdot (\frac{2x}{3}) \\ 3\cdot (x+6) & >4\cdot 2x \\ 3x+18 & >8x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles. 

Remember, when we divide an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+18 & >8x \\ 3x+18-8x & >8x-8x \\ 18-5x & >0 \\ 18-5x-18 & >0-18 \\ -5x & >-18 \\ \frac{-5x}{-5} & \,\,<\,\,\frac{-18}{-5} \\ x & <\frac{18}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x<\frac{18}{5}.$
